title: Falling-Block & Puzzle
blurb: Tetris came in the box when the Game Boy launched in Europe, and puzzle games never really left. This chapter collects the best of them, from Nintendo’s own classics to a Japanese warehouse puzzle and a hero who started out as a potato.

games.title: Tetris
games.blurb: The cartridge that came in the box when the Game Boy launched in Europe in September 1990. The handheld rights went to Dutch-born Henk Rogers, after Britain’s Mirrorsoft lost the race in Moscow. The story was (in my opinion) brilliantly dramatised in the 2023 film <cite>Tetris</cite>. Creator Alexey Pajitnov still calls this his favourite version of his own game.

games.title: Kwirk
games.blurb: Known as <cite>Puzzle Boy</cite> in Japan, where the hero was a potato. For the West he became a tomato called Kwirk. Nintendo itself published it in Europe, and <cite>Mean Machines</cite> gave it 85%.

games.title: Boxxle
games.blurb: A Game Boy version of <cite>Sokoban</cite>, the Japanese “warehouse keeper” puzzle that spawned a whole game genre. It was one of the very first third-party Game Boy games, with 108 levels and a level editor. FCI brought it to Europe in 1991.

games.title: Dr. Mario
games.blurb: Not a Miyamoto game, despite the name! Gunpei Yokoi’s team made it. It reached Europe in April 1991, seven months after the Game Boy itself. Clear four combos in a row and you’ll hear a snippet of Mario’s invincibility music.

games.title: Mario & Yoshi
games.blurb: Known simply as <cite>Yoshi</cite> in America. Swap the plates to stack falling enemies, then catch the eggshells to hatch a Yoshi! It sold well enough to help Game Freak on its way to its next big idea: Pokémon.

games.title: Yoshi’s Cookie
games.blurb: Line up rows and columns of cookies, with Yoshi as the wild card. Henk Rogers licensed the idea from a failed arcade game called Hermetica, and the Game Boy version still mentions that name in its hidden debug menu.

games.title: Mario’s Picross
games.blurb: Mario as an archaeologist, chiselling pictures out of number grids. It didn’t sell well in Europe or America, so its Game Boy sequel stayed in Japan. <cite>Total!</cite> still gave it 80%, and called it “instantly addictive”. I’m inclined to agree.

games.title: Tetris Attack
games.blurb: Actually has nothing to do with <cite>Tetris</cite>: you swap coloured panels to make lines and set off chain reactions. The Super Famicom original starred fairies, but the Game Boy version is Yoshi-themed even in Japan. You can unlock six hidden Super Game Boy borders with button codes on the title screen.

games.title: Kirby’s Star Stacker
games.blurb: Kirby’s animal friends Rick, Kine and Coo help clear stars in this falling-block puzzler. It was the last Kirby game made for the original Game Boy. Japan later got a Super Famicom remake that never left the country.

title: Mario, Wario, Kirby & Kong
blurb: Nintendo’s mascots on the go! Mario launched alongside the Game Boy in Europe, Wario made his debut on it, and Kirby was born here too. Then British studio Rare managed to squeeze <cite>Donkey Kong Country</cite> onto it, which is quite impressive.

games.title: Super Mario Land
games.blurb: Mario’s first handheld adventure, and one of the first games you could buy when the Game Boy launched in Europe in September 1990. It even inspired a UK top ten hit: “Supermarioland” by Ambassadors of Funk. Nintendo UK loved it, but the song never came out in America.

games.title: Super Mario Land 2: 6 Golden Coins
games.blurb: A big leap from the first game, with a world map and Wario’s first appearance. Britain got it in November 1992, a few months before the rest of Europe. Nintendo UK’s print ads took a cheeky swipe at Sega: “Why did the Hedgehog cross the road?”

games.title: Wario Land: Super Mario Land 3
games.blurb: The subtitle says Mario, but Wario steals the show. He collects treasure to buy his own castle, and your coin total decides how grand it gets, from a palace to a birdhouse. In the UK it was the best-selling Game Boy game for three months in 1994.

games.title: Wario Land II
games.blurb: Wario can’t die in this one. Getting hit squashes him flat or sets him on fire, which is often how you solve the level! Japan only got the Game Boy Color version, so this grey cartridge only came out in America and Europe.

games.title: Kirby’s Dream Land
games.blurb: Kirby’s debut, and the first game designed by Masahiro Sakurai. During development he was called Popopo, and early boxes were even printed as <cite>Twinkle Popo</cite>. There are no copy abilities yet: you simply suck up enemies and spit them back out. But even that was novel for the time!

games.title: Kirby’s Dream Land 2
games.blurb: Kirby’s copy abilities arrive on Game Boy, together with three animal friends: Rick the hamster, Kine the fish and Coo the owl. Europe got it in July 1995. On a Super Game Boy, the ending uses every colour it can to paint a rainbow.

games.title: Donkey Kong
games.blurb: It starts as the 1981 arcade game, with its four famous stages. Then it keeps going, with 97 brand-new puzzle levels. It was the first game designed for the Super Game Boy, and in the UK it was the best-selling Game Boy game in the autumn of 1994.

games.title: Donkey Kong Land
games.blurb: Rare didn’t simply port <cite>Donkey Kong Country</cite>. Programmer Paul Machacek convinced co-founder Tim Stamper to make a brand-new game instead. It came on a banana-yellow cartridge, and <cite>CVG</cite> even called it better than the SNES original.

games.title: Donkey Kong Land 2
games.blurb: Diddy and Dixie’s adventure from <cite>Donkey Kong Country 2</cite>, rebuilt for the Game Boy by Rare. The levels are shorter and the colours are gone, but it still feels like proper <cite>Donkey Kong Country</cite>. It reached in November 1996, two months after America.

title: Capcom & Konami Action
blurb: Capcom and Konami ruled the NES, and they brought their heroes along to the Game Boy. Expect whips, robot masters and a bionic arm, plus Nintendo’s own <cite>Kid Icarus</cite> and a ninja that Europe once again knew from <cite>Shadow Warriors</cite>.

games.title: Castlevania: The Adventure
games.blurb: The very first handheld <cite>Castlevania</cite>, starring Christopher Belmont, Simon’s ancestor. There are no sub-weapons, and every hit downgrades your whip. It’s famously slow, but <cite>Total!</cite> said that didn’t spoil the fun. Europe later even got it in colour, in <cite>Konami GB Collection Vol. 1</cite>.

games.title: Castlevania II: Belmont’s Revenge
games.blurb: Fifteen years later, Christopher returns to rescue his son Soleil from Dracula. You can play the first four castles in any order, just like in <cite>Mega Man</cite>. The Western release swapped the cross for an axe, but Europe’s <cite>Konami GB Collection Vol. 4</cite> brought it back, in colour.

games.title: Bionic Commando
games.blurb: A Game Boy remake of the NES classic, with the story moved to a sci-fi future. You still can’t jump: your bionic arm is the only way up. It was made by Minakuchi Engineering, the same studio behind both Game Boy <cite>Mega Man</cite> games in this chapter.

games.title: Kid Icarus: Of Myths and Monsters
games.blurb: Pit’s second adventure, and a sequel to the NES original. Nintendo made it in Japan but never released it there: Japanese players only got it in 2012, on the 3DS. <cite>Nintendo Magazine System</cite> was less impressed, giving it 71% and calling it “long in the tooth”.

games.title: Mega Man: Dr. Wily’s Revenge
games.blurb: Mega Man’s handheld debut, mixing robot masters from the first two NES games. It was also the first <cite>Mega Man</cite> game Capcom handed to an outside studio. Europe got it in January 1992, and German cartridges even had their own title: <cite>Dr. Wily’s Rache</cite>.

games.title: Mega Man V
games.blurb: My favourite of the five Game Boy <cite>Mega Man</cite> games, with brand-new bosses from space: the Stardroids. Mega Man gets a rocket fist called the Mega Arm, and a robot cat called Tango. It came out in Europe in November 1994, a full year before <cite>Mega Man IV</cite>. PAL copies are now highly sought after.

games.title: Shadow Warriors
games.blurb: It started life as a Game Boy version of Natsume’s <cite>Blue Shadow</cite>, until Tecmo bought the rights and turned it into a <cite>Ninja Gaiden</cite> prequel. The villain, Emperor Garuda, still comes from <cite>Blue Shadow</cite>. In Europe, Ryu’s NES games were already called <cite>Shadow Warriors</cite>, so this one was too. <cite>CVG</cite> gave it 90%.

title: Adventures & RPGs
blurb: Hardly any Japanese RPGs came out in Europe during this era, so adventures and role-playing games share a chapter here. Link and Samus are joined by the very first <cite>Mana</cite> game, and by the two Pokémon games that swept through Europe’s schoolyards in 1999.

games.title: Blaster Master Jr.
games.blurb: Despite the name, Jason leaves his tank at home! This is really a sequel to Hudson’s <cite>RoboWarrior</cite>, a <cite>Bomberman</cite> spin-off, given a <cite>Blaster Master</cite> makeover for the West. Europe even got it before America.

games.title: Gargoyle’s Quest
games.blurb: Firebrand, the gargoyle who made Ghosts ’n Goblins so damn hard, gets an adventure of his own. It mixes side-scrolling action with a top-down RPG map, and Nintendo itself published it in Europe. Its NES prequel, Gargoyle’s Quest II, is in the NES Collection.

games.title: Metroid II: Return of Samus
games.blurb: Samus has to wipe out every last Metroid on their home planet, SR388. Europe got it on 21 May 1992, the same day as <cite>Kid Icarus</cite>. <cite>Total!</cite> complained about large, empty areas, which I think is fair criticism. But its ending leads straight into <cite>Super Metroid</cite>!

games.title: The Sword of Hope
games.blurb: A fantasy adventure where you explore by picking commands from a menu, instead of walking around. It comes from Kemco, the company behind the NES versions of <cite>Shadowgate</cite> and <cite>Déjà Vu</cite>. In Europe, it only came out in Swedish, Spanish and German.

games.title: The Legend of Zelda: Link’s Awakening
games.blurb: Link washes up on Koholint Island, and director Takashi Tezuka wanted it to feel like the TV series <cite>Twin Peaks</cite>. Look out for cameos by Yoshi, Kirby and Dr. Wright from <cite>SimCity</cite>. There’s even a prince from <cite>Kaeru no Tame ni Kane wa Naru</cite>, the Japan-only game whose engine this Zelda was built on.

games.title: Mystic Quest
games.blurb: Known as <cite>Final Fantasy Adventure</cite> in America, and the first <cite>Mana</cite> game. Europe got it in June 1993, without the <cite>Final Fantasy</cite> name. Confusingly, Europe’s version of the SNES game <cite>Final Fantasy Mystic Quest</cite> was renamed as well, to <cite>Mystic Quest Legend</cite>.

games.title: Pokémon Red and Blue
games.blurb: Gotta catch ’em all! Europe had to wait until October 1999, more than three years after Japan and a year after America. It was worth the wait: in France alone, it sold over 2.5 million copies in its first year.

games.title: Pokémon Yellow
games.blurb: <cite>Red</cite> and <cite>Blue</cite> again, but closer to the TV series, with Pikachu following you around. It reached Europe in June 2000. It’s a Game Boy Color-enhanced cartridge, but it plays perfectly well on the DMG. I was 10 at the time, and my friend down the street had it, which made me very jealous!

title: Shoot-’em-ups
blurb: Playing shoot-’em-ups on a tiny greenish screen sounds like a bad idea, but these games prove otherwise. Konami’s <cite>Nemesis</cite> and <cite>Probotector</cite> games lead the way, next to a British-made <cite>R-Type</cite> that Europe got before anyone else.

games.title: R-Type
games.blurb: Japanese studios reportedly turned this conversion down, convinced it couldn’t be done. The job went to British studio Bits, where Jas Austin squeezed the arcade game onto a small cartridge by cutting two levels. It reached Europe in December 1990, months before Japan and America, and it won a Golden Joystick.

games.title: R-Type II
games.blurb: Bits returned for the sequel, this time with Bob Pape programming. He’d already managed to fit the first <cite>R-Type</cite> onto the ZX Spectrum, so he was the right man for the job.

games.title: Solar Striker
games.blurb: Nintendo’s own vertical shooter, and one of the games on the shelves when the Game Boy launched in Europe. German magazine <cite>Power Play</cite> liked its variety, but couldn’t ignore how simple it was. <cite>Mean Machines</cite> gave it just 69%.

games.title: Nemesis
games.blurb: The first <cite>Gradius</cite> game on the DMG. It sold everywhere under the name Europe knew from the arcades: <cite>Nemesis</cite>. Even Japan got it with that title. <cite>Total!</cite> called it a “superb version of a classic coin-op” and gave it 92%.

games.title: Nemesis II: The Return of the Hero
games.blurb: Called <cite>Gradius: The Interstellar Assault</cite> in America, but Europe kept the <cite>Nemesis</cite> name. It’s a brand-new game made just for the Game Boy. Europe later got it in colour, in <cite>Konami GB Collection Vol. 4</cite>.

games.title: Probotector
games.blurb: Konami’s Game Boy <cite>Contra</cite>, made just for the handheld, with top-down stages between the side-scrolling ones. As always in Europe, the soldiers became robots. Interestingly, when it returned in 2000 in <cite>Konami GB Collection Vol. 1</cite>, it was still called <cite>Probotector</cite>, but the heroes were human again.

games.title: Dropzone
games.blurb: Archer Maclean’s 1984 computer classic, a <cite>Defender</cite>-style shooter where you rescue scientists from alien invaders. British publisher Mindscape brought it to the Game Boy in 1992.

games.title: Parodius
games.blurb: Konami’s cheeky <cite>Gradius</cite> parody. The Game Boy version has eight of the arcade’s stages, and even lists the ages of the playable characters. Like the NES version, it only came out in Japan and Europe. Oddly, the European cartridges carry the name of Ultra Games, Konami’s American label.

title: Fighting & Beat-’em-ups
blurb: Fighting games on a two-button handheld? Somehow, it worked. British studios Probe and Rare handled <cite>Mortal Kombat</cite> and <cite>Killer Instinct</cite>, while Technōs and Konami brought the beat-’em-ups that started it all.

games.title: Double Dragon
games.blurb: Billy and Jimmy’s first handheld outing reached Europe in November 1990, just two months after the Game Boy itself. The American cartridge even warns that it can only be played in the USA and Canada. European players didn’t seem to mind.

games.title: Double Dragon II
games.blurb: In Japan this was a <cite>Kunio-kun</cite> game, from the same series as <cite>River City Ransom</cite>, which Europe knew as <cite>Street Gangs</cite>. For the West, Acclaim turned it into a <cite>Double Dragon</cite> sequel, with Billy and Jimmy taking over. Europe got it in December 1991.

games.title: Teenage Mutant Hero Turtles: Fall of the Foot Clan
games.blurb: The Turtles’ first Game Boy game. You pick a Turtle and fight your way through the Foot Clan to rescue April. <cite>Nintendo Power</cite> later ranked it among the 20 best Game Boy games of all time.

games.title: Battletoads
games.blurb: Same name, different game. Rare made a brand-new <cite>Battletoads</cite> for the Game Boy, with its own levels, and it’s just as brutal. A proper port of the NES game followed in 1993, as <cite>Battletoads in Ragnarok’s World</cite>.

games.title: Mortal Kombat
games.blurb: Released on every console on the same day: “Mortal Monday”, 13 September 1993. Probe had to cut a lot to fit it on a Game Boy cartridge, but it still sold over a million copies on the handheld alone.

games.title: Mortal Kombat II
games.blurb: “Mortal Friday” followed a year later, on 9 September 1994, and Probe returned for the Game Boy version. Unlike the Game Gear version, this one has no blood at all.

games.title: Samurai Shodown
games.blurb: SNK’s sword-fighting classic, ported by Takara. Somehow every character and stage made it onto the cartridge, although the combos and voices didn’t. Critics found it surprisingly good for a Game Boy game.

games.title: Killer Instinct
games.blurb: Rare’s arcade hit crammed into the Game Boy, minus Cinder and Riptor. <cite>EGM</cite> said it “should never have been attempted on the Game Boy”. On a Super Game Boy, though, you get colour, plus a proper two-player mode with a second controller.

games.title: Street Fighter II
games.blurb: The Game Boy only has two buttons, so how hard you punch or kick depends on how long you hold them. Nintendo itself published it in Europe in 1995. <cite>EGM</cite> found it “lethargically slow”, but still an impressive conversion.

games.title: The King of Fighters ’95
games.blurb: Europe got this one in August 1996, half a year before America. Gaibrain squeezed SNK’s team fighter onto the Game Boy, and there’s even a secret character: Nakoruru from <cite>Samurai Shodown</cite>.

title: Sports & Racing
blurb: Simple sports games were perfect for a handheld. Nintendo’s own launch games sit next to Konami’s arcade ports, a Rare racer, and the Amiga’s favourite football game.

games.title: Golf
games.blurb: One of the games on the shelves when the Game Boy launched in Europe. Eighteen holes of simple, meter-based golf, but <cite>AllGame</cite> still gave it four stars out of five.

games.title: Tennis
games.blurb: Nintendo’s NES tennis game, shrunk down for the Game Boy, with Mario in the umpire’s chair. Slightly more forgiving than the original, in my opinion. In America it was one of the five launch games, and Europe got it in 1990.

games.title: Blades of Steel
games.blurb: Konami’s arcade-style hockey game, and yes, the fights survived the trip to the Game Boy. It was released in Europe in 1991, more than a year before Japan.

games.title: F-1 Race
games.blurb: Nintendo’s Formula One game supported the Four Player Adapter, so four friends could race each other. Look out for Mario, Link, Samus and other Nintendo stars at the end of the tracks. It was “lights out, and away we go!” in October 1991.

games.title: Motocross Maniacs
games.blurb: A side-on dirt-bike racer full of loops and ramps, with nitro boosts to clear the jumps. It reached Europe in 1991. Sadly, it didn’t have battery-powered save memory, so your best times were gone as soon as you switched off.

games.title: The Spirit of F-1
games.blurb: Konami’s racer was known as <cite>F-1 Spirit</cite> in Japan and <cite>World Circuit Series</cite> in America. Palcom brought it to Europe in 1992. You work your way up from Formula 3 through Formula 3000 to Formula 1, on 25 tracks from around the world.

games.title: Super R.C. Pro-Am
games.blurb: British studio Rare’s Game Boy follow-up to its NES racer, with music by David Wise. It was released in Europe in April 1992, almost a year after America. It went on to sell over a million copies.

games.title: Track & Field
games.blurb: Konami’s button-masher reached Europe in October 1992, just after the Barcelona Olympics. In Japan it was even called <cite>Konami Sports in Barcelona</cite>. Europe later got it in colour, in <cite>Konami GB Collection Vol. 2</cite>.

games.title: Hyperdunk
games.blurb: Konami’s <cite>Double Dribble</cite> on the Game Boy, renamed <cite>Hyperdunk</cite> for Europe. In Japan it was <cite>Konamic Basket</cite>. Later, Konami’s Mega Drive game <cite>Double Dribble: The Playoff Edition</cite> was also sold in Europe as <cite>Hyperdunk</cite>, with this game’s box art, although it’s a completely different game.

games.title: Sensible Soccer
games.blurb: The Amiga’s favourite football game, from Britain’s Sensible Software. On the Game Boy it plays with a single button: how long you hold it decides how hard you shoot. Sony Imagesoft published it in 1994.

games.title: Wave Race
games.blurb: No relation to the later N64 game: this is a top-down jet-ski racer. America got it in 1992, but Europe had to wait five years. In the UK it became a £9.99 budget game, often bundled with the Game Boy Pocket, and Dutch magazine <cite>Power Unlimited</cite> recommended it for “speed enthusiasts who love the Game Boy”.

games.title: International Superstar Soccer
games.blurb: Konami’s football game, known as <cite>World Soccer GB</cite> in Japan. Released in June 1998, we got it months before America. The Japan Football Association logo even appears on the title screen.

title: Licensed & Movie Tie-ins
blurb: Licensed games have a bad reputation, but not all of them deserve it. Sunsoft’s Batman and Capcom’s Disney games are really good, and Europe even got an enjoyable McDonald’s platformer that the rest of the world only knew with a 7 Up mascot.

games.title: Batman: The Video Game
games.blurb: Despite the name, it’s nothing like the NES game, which is great because that game is super hard! Reviewers compared the Game Boy game to <cite>Super Mario Land</cite>, and Batman even carries a gun. European magazines loved it: <cite>Player One</cite> gave it 94% and <cite>Mean Machines</cite> 85%. By the end of 1990 it had sold over half a million copies.

games.title: The Bugs Bunny Crazy Castle
games.blurb: In Japan this was a Mickey Mouse game, and on the Famicom it starred Roger Rabbit. Kemco simply swapped the licence for each market. Its sequel became <cite>Hugo</cite> in Europe, and in 2021 a young LeBron James even plays it in <cite>Space Jam: A New Legacy</cite>.

games.title: DuckTales
games.blurb: Scrooge’s pogo cane works just as well on the Game Boy, with the same five treasure hunts as the NES game, Moon included. Europe got it in 1991, and British magazine <cite>Raze</cite> gave it 90%.

games.title: Alien 3
games.blurb: Unlike every other version, the Game Boy <cite>Alien 3</cite> is a top-down game, made by Bits. It reached Europe in December 1992. Dutch and Belgian shops sold the German version, with a simple black-and-white sheet of Dutch and French instructions.

games.title: McDonaldland
games.blurb: This game only exists like this in Europe. America got the exact same game a couple of months later as <cite>Spot: The Cool Adventure</cite>, with 7 Up’s mascot Spot instead of Ronald McDonald. Dutch magazine <cite>Power Unlimited</cite> gave it 68%.

games.title: Tiny Toon Adventures: Babs’ Big Break
games.blurb: Montana Max wants to tear down the Acme Theatre, so Buster, Plucky and Hamton race to warn Babs before her big break. European magazines loved it: France’s <cite>Joystick</cite> gave it 93%, and <cite>Total!</cite> and <cite>Nintendo Magazine System</cite> both gave it 89%.

games.title: Darkwing Duck
games.blurb: Capcom’s NES adventure, shrunk down for the Game Boy, and <cite>Nintendo Power</cite>’s third-best Game Boy game of 1993. In Europe it came out in English, German and Spanish versions. <cite>Nintendo Magazine System</cite> called it “entertaining and varied”.

games.title: Aladdin
games.blurb: Made by British studio NMS Software and published by Virgin. Europe got it in September 1994, more than a year before America. <cite>CVG</cite> found it a bit ordinary next to the 16-bit versions, but on a Super Game Boy it does get a splash of colour.

title: Comic Heroes from Europe
blurb: Europe grew up on comic albums, not superhero comics. French publisher Infogrames brought Asterix, the Smurfs, Tintin, Spirou and Lucky Luke to the Game Boy, and most of them were made in Barcelona. Hardly any of them ever left Europe.

games.title: Asterix
games.blurb: Bit Managers’ first <cite>Asterix</cite> game came out on Game Boy in the summer of 1993, a few months before the NES version. It only ever came out in Europe, with text in English, French, German and Spanish. French magazine <cite>Joypad</cite> gave it 91%.

games.title: Asterix & Obelix
games.blurb: This time you can play as Asterix or Obelix, each with his own moves. To fit four languages in, Infogrames made two versions of the cartridge: one in English and Spanish, and one in French and German.

games.title: The Smurfs
games.blurb: One of the first games with a language menu: you could play it in English, French, German or Spanish. America got it a year later, in a revised version with Super Game Boy support that later reached European shops too. The revision quietly dropped Spanish, though.

games.title: Spirou
games.blurb: The Belgian bellboy’s only Game Boy adventure, made by Bit Managers and released only in Europe. Critics loved the animation and how faithful it was to the comic, but warned that it was hard, with only one password to save your progress.

games.title: Tintin in Tibet
games.blurb: Tintin follows his friend Chang’s trail into the Himalayas, based on Hergé’s famous album. Bit Managers made the Game Boy version, which only came out in Europe. French magazine <cite>Consoles+</cite> gave it 90%.

games.title: Lucky Luke
games.blurb: The man who shoots faster than his shadow, on a Game Boy cartridge by French studio Velez & Dubail. It came out in Europe in 1997, two years before a separate Game Boy Color game.

title: Arcade, Pinball & Party
blurb: Not everything needs to be an epic adventure. These are arcade classics, pinball tables and party games: perfect for a quick round on the bus, or a link-cable battle with a friend.

games.title: Qix
games.blurb: Taito’s territory-grabbing arcade game, published by Nintendo itself and one of Europe’s very first Game Boy games. Between rounds, Mario, Luigi and Princess Peach make little cameo appearances.

games.title: Bubble Bobble
games.blurb: Bub and Bob’s bubble-blowing classic, squeezed onto the Game Boy by Taito itself. Europe got it first, in November 1991, a couple of months before America.

games.title: Chase H.Q.
games.blurb: Europe already loved Ocean’s <cite>Chase H.Q.</cite> on home computers, where it won a Golden Joystick. Taito’s own Game Boy version followed in 1991: catch up with the criminal before time runs out, then ram his car until he gives up.

games.title: Elevator Action
games.blurb: A spy game from 1983: ride the lifts, shoot out the lights and grab the secret documents before you escape. Taito’s Game Boy version reached Europe in December 1991.

games.title: Kirby’s Pinball Land
games.blurb: Kirby himself is the ball, bouncing across three tables, each with a boss at the top. Europe got this one on 1 December 1993, just one day after America. Still counts!

games.title: Kirby’s Block Ball
games.blurb: <cite>Breakout</cite>-but-Kirby! Kirby is the ball, and his copy abilities change how he smashes through the blocks. <cite>Nintendo World Report</cite> called it the best version of <cite>Breakout</cite> ever made. On a Super Game Boy it gets a themed border and lots of colour.

games.title: Pinball Dreams
games.blurb: Based on the Amiga pinball classic by Swedish studio Digital Illusions, who later became DICE. British studio Spidersoft managed to put three of its four tables onto the Game Boy, just leaving out Beat Box. Dutch magazine <cite>Power Unlimited</cite> gave it 85%.

games.title: Wario Blast: Featuring Bomberman!
games.blurb: In Japan this is simply <cite>Bomberman GB</cite>, but in the West Wario muscled his way in. Europe got it in June 1995, and with a Super Game Boy and a multitap, four players could battle on one TV. <cite>Games World</cite> gave it 86%.

games.title: Game & Watch Gallery
games.blurb: Four Game & Watch classics, each in an original and a modern version starring Mario and friends. Collect enough stars and you unlock a gallery of other Game & Watch games. Europe got it in August 1997.

title: Home-Computer Hits
blurb: The NES got a handful of computer classics, but the Game Boy got even more. These are the games Europe’s computer kids already knew, from Boulder Dash to Lemmings, and many of them were converted by British studios.

games.title: Boulder Dash
games.blurb: Australian studio Beam Software converted it, and it never came out in America at all. Japan got it first, with penguins and jellyfish added to Rockford’s caves. <cite>Mean Machines</cite> gave it 90%, calling it “one of the finest video games ever written”.

games.title: Bubble Ghost
games.blurb: French studio ERE Informatique’s Atari ST hit: you blow a fragile bubble through a haunted castle. Japan’s Opera House made the Game Boy version, with one of the very first scores by Hitoshi Sakimoto, who became famous for <cite>Final Fantasy Tactics</cite>. European players got it in 1992, two years after America.

games.title: Prince of Persia
games.blurb: Jordan Mechner’s classic: you have one hour to rescue the princess. The European cartridge lets you pick from five languages, and its music was the very first video game work of Tommy Tallarico, later known for <cite>Earthworm Jim</cite>.

games.title: Speedball 2: Brutal Deluxe
games.blurb: The Bitmap Brothers’ brutal future sport, converted by Spidersoft, who also did <cite>Pinball Dreams</cite>. Spidersoft later became part of Rockstar, as Rockstar Lincoln. The Amiga original’s music even won a Golden Joystick!

games.title: Turrican
games.blurb: Manfred Trenz’s German computer hero, converted by British studio The Code Monkeys and released in Europe in spring 1992. Accolade later reworked this Game Boy version into <cite>Universal Soldier</cite>, a film tie-in.

games.title: Lemmings
games.blurb: Ocean brought DMA Design’s Scottish hit to the Game Boy, and Europe got it in January 1993, more than a year and a half before America. Guiding lemmings to the exit is a lot harder on a screen this small.

games.title: Spy vs Spy
games.blurb: The <cite>Mad</cite> magazine spies, back on a Nintendo handheld. America got it in 1992, but Europe only got it in March 1997, five years later. Set your traps, grab the briefcase, and escape before the other spy does! Such a cool game.

title: Cult Classics & Deep Cuts
blurb: The strange, the rare and the overlooked. Some of these are now expensive collector’s items, one is a Danish TV troll in disguise, and one was made in Britain and reached Europe before anyone else.

games.title: Amazing Penguin
games.blurb: Known in Japan as <cite>Osawagase! Penguin Boy</cite>. Prince Pendrich clears each maze by tracing its panels, kicking enemies out of the way. A small, overlooked Natsume original.

games.title: Avenging Spirit
games.blurb: You play as a ghost who can possess almost any enemy, using their powers to rescue your kidnapped girlfriend. Jaleco brought it to Europe in 1992, and it became such a cult favourite that Limited Run Games reissued it on cartridge in 2022.

games.title: Alfred Chicken
games.blurb: A British original: the Game Boy version came first, before the Amiga and SNES ports. Mindscape released it in Europe in 1993, months before America and two years before Japan. The music is by David Whittaker, who also did the sound for <cite>R-Type</cite> on Game Boy.

games.title: Kid Dracula
games.blurb: Konami’s own cute parody of <cite>Castlevania</cite>, starring Dracula’s son. It was released in Europe in March 1993, identical to the American version. Today, cartridges sell for between £75 and over £300, according to <cite>Retro Gamer</cite>.

games.title: Trip World
games.blurb: Sunsoft’s gentle platformer starring Yakopoo, a little bunny-like creature. It came out in Japan and Europe but never in America, with Britain getting it in June 1993. So few copies were made that boxed cartridges are now expensive collector’s items.

games.title: Hugo
games.blurb: The Danish TV troll’s Game Boy debut is secretly Kemco’s Crazy Castle 2, the sequel to the Bugs Bunny game in chapter 8. Europe had already got this exact game in 1992, released simply as Mickey Mouse. So Europe got it twice, under two different licences. Hugo has to rescue his wife Hugolina, and this is the only version of the game with Super Game Boy support.

games.title: Mole Mania
games.blurb: Muddy the mole digs between the surface and the underground to solve puzzles and rescue his family. Shigeru Miyamoto produced it, and Pax Softnica, also behind <cite>Wave Race</cite>, developed it with Nintendo. German <cite>Total!</cite> called the idea “not only new, but also surprisingly good”.
